insight: Einarsson v. Canada (ICSID UNCT/20/6) is the first publicly documented ISDS case resting centrally on proprietary data (marine seismic survey data) asserted as a trade-secret and copyright-protected investment under NAFTA Chapter 11; challenged measure is Canada's regulatory disclosure regime (Canada Petroleum Resources Act); jurisdictional objection is the NAFTA Article 1121 waiver requirement. Merits hearing concluded March 2025; award pending. Structurally analogous to the three-ring pattern but in the oil-and-gas sector, not pharma.

The USMCA effectively eliminated ISDS between Canada and the United States; the three-year legacy period expired 30 June 2023, foreclosing any successor to Eli Lilly v. Canada under the principal North American framework. No pharmaceutical IP ISDS claim against Canada can now be filed by a US investor under any USMCA provision.

No publicly known ISDS case has been filed or decided with pharmaceutical trade secrets or clinical trial data as the primary covered investment. The Ferguson/Kim framework remains theoretical and unlitigated. Einarsson (non-pharma data) is the nearest structural analogue.

China's NMPA Implementation Measures for Drug Trial Data Protection (effective May 2026) create formal, protectable, and tradable entitlements in pharmaceutical clinical trial data and marketing authorisation certificates — establishing the Ring 1 foundation for potential future ISDS claims under China's BIT network if protections are subsequently restricted or unevenly applied.

Jason Yu Song v. China (PCA 2019-39, Final Award January 2025) reveals a structural gap in Denial of Benefits clause architecture: existing DOB clauses address corporate third-country nationality but not natural persons who acquire citizenship to access treaty protection. China's nationality-planning argument failed on admissibility (time-bar); the doctrinal gap remains unaddressed.

The CPTPP also forecloses a direct ISDS pathway for pharmaceutical clinical data exclusivity claims: the TPP's data exclusivity obligations for pharmaceutical undisclosed test data (Art. 18.50 of the original TPP) were suspended when the US withdrew, and Chapter 18 IP obligations cannot be directly enforced via ISDS in any event (only Chapter 9 Section A investment standards can). No pharmaceutical IP ISDS case has been filed under CPTPP. UK accession (December 2024) adds investor pool but does not restore suspended provisions. Combined with the USMCA closure, both principal multilateral frameworks available to pharmaceutical investors now lack a direct clinical-data ISDS hook.

The China-Switzerland BIT (2009) explicitly includes 'know-how' in its investment definition (alongside copyrights, patents, and trade marks), making it the most legally specific existing treaty vehicle for asserting pharmaceutical clinical trial data as a covered investment against China. 'Know-how' is the natural treaty characterisation of confidential proprietary research data and does not depend on domestic trade-secret or copyright law. Combined with China's NMPA 2026 pharmaceutical data exclusivity framework, this BIT provides the most credible existing three-ring pathway for the Ferguson/Kim clinical data scenario, with Swiss pharmaceutical investors (Roche, Novartis, Lonza) as the most plausible future claimants.

NAFTA Article 1121's waiver-consistency requirement constitutes a second, independent Ring 3 jurisdictional mechanism in data-as-investment cases, distinct from the Philip Morris abuse-of-rights pattern. The claimant must not only file a written waiver of parallel proceedings but must act consistently with it. Failure to do so — i.e., continuing to pursue damages claims in domestic forums after submission — deprives the tribunal of jurisdiction (Waste Management I, Detroit International Bridge). Canada's Art. 1121 objection in Einarsson v. Canada (UNCT/20/6) invokes exactly this: if sustained, the tribunal is dismissed without reaching the data-as-investment question. This mechanism turns on the claimant's post-waiver litigation conduct, not on corporate restructuring or treaty-shopping.

UNCITRAL WG III denial-of-benefits reform is converging on a July 2026 Commission deliverable focused on procedural elements (Draft Provision 9 in WP.253, renumbered from Draft Provision 17). The 9th intersessional (November 2025, Santiago) and 53rd session (January 2026, New York) confirm the trajectory: 'feasible over transformative.' The natural-person nationality-planning gap revealed by Jason Yu Song v. China is not confirmed as addressed by any draft provision and is very unlikely to be included in the July 2026 package. Ring 3 doctrine architecture unchanged pending July 2026 Commission outcome.

The China-Germany BIT (2003) explicitly includes 'trade and business secrets' in its Article 1 investment definition — alongside 'know-how,' 'technical processes,' and other IP categories — making it the most legally direct existing treaty-text vehicle for asserting pharmaceutical trade secrets as a covered investment against China. This goes beyond the China-Switzerland BIT (2009) ('know-how' only) and matches the Ferguson/Kim framework's core concept most precisely. The China-France BIT (2007) also covers 'know-how.' Combined, all three major European pharmaceutical investor home states (Germany: Bayer, Merck KGaA; Switzerland: Roche, Novartis; France: Sanofi) now have documented treaty-text Ring 1 bases under their China BITs. European BIT architecture survey complete.

The UNCITRAL 59th Commission session (June 29–July 10, 2026, New York) opens in three days — the milestone T05 has been tracking. The Commission deliverable is A/CN.9/1246 ('Draft supplementary provisions on the conduct of proceedings'), a procedural Protocol only: evidence, bifurcation, interim measures, manifest lack of legal merit, security for costs, TPF disclosure, counterclaims, cost allocation. The denial-of-benefits provision (Draft Provision 9, WP.253) is NOT in A/CN.9/1246. The natural-person nationality-planning gap from Jason Yu Song v. China (PCA 2019-39) is not addressed by the July 2026 Commission package. Ring 3 doctrine architecture is unchanged pending the session outcome (expected by July 10, 2026).

The 2026 USTR Special 301 Report (May 2026) formally characterises China's pharmaceutical trial data protection conditions as imposing 'unfair and discriminatory conditions on the effective protection against unfair commercial use, as well as unauthorized disclosure, of undisclosed test or other data generated to obtain marketing approval for pharmaceutical products.' The specific discriminatory gap: China's final measures do not address the protection period for drugs first approved outside China — disadvantaging exactly the European multinational originators (Bayer, Merck KGaA, Roche, Novartis, Sanofi) who are the most plausible Ring 1 BIT claimants. The US has no BIT with China and cannot pursue ISDS; European BIT holders can, and could reference the USTR characterisation to corroborate a Ring 2 discriminatory treatment argument under the China-Germany (2003), China-Switzerland (2009), or China-France (2007) BITs. This is the first identified government-level characterisation of China's pharmaceutical data conditions as potentially discriminatory — converging the Ring 1 foundation (NMPA 2026 measures creating the investment) with the Ring 2 trigger (discriminatory application). Additionally, the June 5, 2026 transitional deadline has passed: companies that failed to submit data protection requests to China's CDE by that date have definitively waived pharmaceutical data exclusivity rights, crystallising which investors hold formal entitlements that could found a BIT claim.

Hela Schwarz GmbH v. People's Republic of China (ICSID ARB/17/19), final award December 10, 2025, is the first decided ICSID case under the China-Germany BIT (2003) — the treaty identified as the primary Ring 1 vehicle for pharmaceutical trade secrets. The tribunal dismissed all EUR 90+ million claims on both jurisdiction and merits grounds. The jurisdictional ground is the BIT's concurrent-proceedings / court-withdrawal requirement: because the claimant's Chinese subsidiary had filed the same claim before Chinese domestic courts before the ICSID arbitration was commenced, the tribunal held the arbitration invalid. This constitutes a third Ring 3 mechanism for the China pharmaceutical data ISDS scenario, distinct from the Philip Morris critical-date / abuse-of-rights doctrine and the NAFTA Art. 1121 waiver mechanism. A European pharmaceutical investor seeking to challenge a Chinese NMPA pharmaceutical data exclusivity decision under the China-Germany BIT (2003) must first withdraw any concurrent Chinese administrative appeals or court proceedings before filing at ICSID — a step that conflicts with the investor's natural first resort to domestic remedies. Counsel for China: A&O Shearman + Ministry of Commerce. Presiding Arbitrator: Sir Daniel Bethlehem KC. Specific BIT article unconfirmed (PDF blocked); holding confirmed from CDR News, A&O Shearman, italaw, and UNCTAD Navigator at high confidence.

The Swedish Supreme Court ruled on June 26, 2026 (reversing the Svea Court of Appeal's November 12, 2024 annulment) that an MFN clause in a bilateral investment treaty can confer tribunal competence by importing a more favourable dispute resolution provision from another BIT. Procedural chain: (1) SCC Partial Final Award on Jurisdiction (August 31, 2022) — MFN allowed, SCC jurisdiction upheld by tribunal; (2) Svea Court of Appeal (November 12, 2024) — MFN cannot import forum from another treaty, award annulled; (3) Swedish Supreme Court (leave granted September 22, 2025; ruling June 26, 2026) — reversed, MFN CAN confer forum competence. The underlying dispute (Zaza Okuashvili v. Georgia, SCC Case No. V 2019/058) is a Georgian tax/expropriation claim by a dual Georgian-British national — no IP content. Ring 3 significance: confirms that dual-national investors excluded from ICSID may use MFN clauses to access alternative forums (SCC arbitration under a third BIT) in SCC-seated, Swedish-law arbitrations — a marginal expansion of the Ring 3 jurisdictional toolkit. Full ruling text (NJA citation) not accessible; existence and holding confirmed at medium-high confidence from Swedish Supreme Court news service (search-engine-recovered snippet, June 26, 2026) and IAReporter headline (June 29, 2026).

Three pre-session sources not previously in the project record — EJIL:Talk 'UNCITRAL and ISDS Reform: Moving to the Delivery Phase' (June 2026), ICLRC.ru 'draft provisions on ISDS-specific arbitration procedures almost finalised,' and Kluwer Arbitration Blog's Inaugural Washington Arbitration Week post (May/June 2026) — converge on a more definitive characterisation of the 59th Commission session (opened June 29, 2026): the UNCITRAL reform process has entered its 'delivery phase' and the Procedural Protocol (A/CN.9/1246) is expected to be adopted, not merely considered. The code of conduct for arbitrators and Advisory Centre statute were already adopted in prior sessions; the Protocol completes the programme. For Ring 3: even adoption of the Protocol would not address the denial-of-benefits provision (Draft Provision 9) or the natural-person nationality-planning gap (Jason Yu Song scenario). Those structural gaps in Ring 3 doctrine persist regardless of the session outcome. Day 1 proceedings coverage not available (session opened 10:30 a.m. June 29; real-time indexing lag expected).

Zaza Okuashvili v. Georgia (SCC Case No. V2019/058): the Swedish Supreme Court (June 15, 2026) reversed the Svea Court of Appeal (November 12, 2024) and held that the MFN clause in Article 3(3) of the Georgia-UK BIT (1995) — which explicitly extends MFN treatment to all provisions in Articles 1–11, including Article 8 on dispute settlement — allows a dual Georgian-British investor to import multi-forum arbitral access (including SCC) from the Georgia-BLEU BIT, thereby establishing SCC jurisdiction over a case where the home BIT designated ICSID as the exclusive forum (unavailable to the investor as a Georgian national). This is the first Swedish Supreme Court ruling establishing MFN-forum-access in investment arbitration as a jurisdictional mechanism for dual nationals. No IP nexus (tobacco sector, tax enforcement measure); Ring 3 near-miss — enriches the background MFN + dual-nationality jurisdictional admissibility landscape without advancing the pharmaceutical trade secret or clinical data thread specifically. Outcome confirmed; full judgment text paywalled (IAReporter).

A/CN.9/1246 (UNCITRAL, April 15, 2026 advance copy) does not finalize the temporal scope of its supplementary provisions but uses April 1, 2027 as an illustrative example ('they could apply, for example, to treaties concluded on or after 1 April 2027, if [certain conditions relating to] UARs are met') while noting the scope-of-application provision 'may need to be developed.' The Protocol's non-retroactivity was therefore not a finalized provision in the draft submitted to the Commission; the temporal scope was a live question at the 59th Commission session (June 29–July 10, 2026). Additionally, A/CN.9/1246 explicitly proposes a Mauritius Convention-type opt-in mechanism to make the Protocol applicable to pre-existing investment treaties — meaning the China-Germany BIT (2003), China-Switzerland BIT (2009), and China-France BIT (2007) are not definitively excluded from Protocol coverage if the relevant parties opt in via a future Mauritius-type convention. This corrects the prior framing (which treated the April 1, 2027 date as a confirmed cutoff) and adds the Mauritius opt-in dimension as a live architectural possibility documented within the draft.

Confirmed from practitioner and academic secondary sources (MEDIUM confidence) that Chinese BITs explicitly exclude MFN extension to procedural ISDS rights — the Okuashvili MFN-forum-bypass mechanism (Swedish SC, June 2026) is architecturally closed for European pharmaceutical investors under the China-Germany BIT (2003), China-Switzerland BIT (2009), and China-France BIT (2007). Four-mechanism Ring 3 taxonomy now complete: (1) Philip Morris abuse-of-rights/critical-date [applicable to China BIT scenario]; (2) NAFTA Art. 1121 waiver-consistency [NAFTA/CUSMA-specific; inapplicable to China BITs]; (3) Hela Schwarz concurrent-proceedings/court-withdrawal [directly applicable — China-Germany BIT]; (4) Okuashvili MFN-scope bypass [CLOSED — Chinese BITs exclude MFN from ISDS]. For China pharmaceutical BIT scenario: only mechanisms 1 and 3 are operative Ring 3 gates.

China SAMR Order No. 126 (Provisions on the Protection of Trade Secrets, issued February 24, 2026, effective June 1, 2026) — the most substantial overhaul of China's administrative trade secret enforcement framework in approximately 30 years — explicitly includes 'data, algorithms, and computer program code' as categories of technical information eligible for trade secret protection. Article 29 establishes extraterritorial reach. Administrative enforcement: injunctions and fines up to 5M RMB (no damages). Pharmaceutical clinical trial data falls within the broadened 'data' category by inclusion; the Provisions do not specifically address pharmaceutical or clinical data. This creates a parallel administrative enforcement channel for pharmaceutical trade secrets running alongside the NMPA Implementation Measures for Drug Trial Data Protection (effective May 15, 2026). For the China-Germany BIT (2003)'s 'trade and business secrets' investment-definition language, China's own administrative law now formally characterizes data as a protectable trade secret. [Analytical inference: no practitioner source connects SAMR Order No. 126 to ISDS or BIT investment definitions; regulatory facts confirmed from multiple secondary sources at medium-high confidence; Provisions text not directly read.]

Wingtech Technology (China) / Yuching Holding Limited (HK) issued a formal notice of dispute under the China-Netherlands BIT (Article 10(3)) on October 15, 2025, seeking USD ~8 billion in damages over the Dutch government's emergency order (Goods Availability Act, September 2025) preventing transfer of 'intellectual property rights' and production assets to China. This is the first confirmed Ring 1–2 near-miss under the China–European BIT network since the project began monitoring: IP/technology assets are the central protected investment; the governmental measure directly targets IP transfer. The China-Netherlands BIT contains no national security carve-out — architecturally parallel to the China-Germany BIT (2003) that governs the pharmaceutical trade-secret scenario in reverse. The six-month cooling-off period expired ~April 15, 2026; ICSID formal filing is unconfirmed. The claimant's 'multi-track legal strategy' (parallel Enterprise Chamber domestic proceedings + BIT notice) mirrors the concurrent-proceedings structure that caused Hela Schwarz v. China to fail on jurisdiction. [Inverse scenario: Chinese investor, European respondent — near-miss, not pharmaceutical. Facts at medium-high confidence from Kluwer, AMS Advocaten, NL Times, CELIS. BIT/Ring relevance is a research inference at medium confidence.]

The Statute of the Advisory Centre on International Investment Dispute Resolution was adopted 'in principle' at the 57th UNCITRAL Commission Session in 2024 — not first adopted at the 59th session (July 2026). The 16-article statute was finalized in 2024; the 59th session concerns operationalization (host country, budget, governance) and preparing the statute for formal UN General Assembly adoption in December 2026. This completes and corrects the three-deliverable reform sequence: (1) Code of Conduct for Arbitrators — 56th session (July 2023, UNGA Res. 78/105); (2) Advisory Centre Statute in principle — 57th session (2024); (3) Procedural Protocol (A/CN.9/1246) — expected 59th session (July 2026). The ISDS reform architecture is further along than the prior record indicated on this point. [Not a Ring 1/2/3 pharmaceutical IP finding; corrects UNCITRAL reform timeline in background architecture context. STATE_OF_THE_ANSWER framing updated.]

Jason Yu Song v. People's Republic of China (PCA 2019-39, China-UK BIT 1986) — the only publicly known ISDS award against China [unverified: claim from CMS-lawnow search summary; may carry qualifications] — survived two Swiss Federal Supreme Court set-aside applications: (1) First challenge (4A_46/2024) dismissed April 17, 2025; (2) Second challenge (4A_528/2024) dismissed June 26, 2025 (published July 21, 2025). The second challenge invoked a Chinese criminal court judgment issued during the arbitration as new evidence that the investment was made illegally, arguing this retroactively deprived the tribunal of jurisdiction. The Swiss FSC rejected both challenges; the award (USD 26,045,613.90 + interest) is definitively final. This documents China's post-award resistance arsenal: (a) standard set-aside application; (b) criminal-conviction-as-illegality-of-investment post-award jurisdictional attack, rejected in Swiss-seated proceedings. No IP nexus (land-rights expropriation, Shanxi Province). Ring 3 relevance: the full challenge sequence a pharmaceutical investor would face in a China BIT claim extends beyond the three pre-ICSID-filing Ring 3 gates (Philip Morris abuse-of-rights; Hela Schwarz fork-in-the-road; MFN-closed) to include this post-award resistance layer. Both known mechanisms — standard set-aside and criminal-conviction illegality attack — have been judicially rejected in the sole decided case.
